1	# The library
2	
3	The library is `Library/` and `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/`, without the compiler's own files there:
4	
5	- In `Library/`: the interpreter's prelude, `FortressLibrary.fss` and `.fsi`, and its other components. The compiler's `CompilerLibrary`, `CompilerAlgebra` and `CompilerSystem` are not part of it. `FortressAst.fss` and `.fsi` are generated from `ProjectFortress/astgen/Fortress.ast`: edit that file, never these two.
6	- In `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/`: `FortressBuiltin`, `NativeArray` and the rest. The compiler's `CompilerBuiltin` is not part of it.
7	- `LibraryBuiltin/AnyType`, the top type, belongs to both libraries. After an edit to it, also take the compiled path's step (`build-and-caches.md`, "After an edit of the library").
8	- `Library/incomplete/` is not on the source path (`default_repository/configuration`), so no program can import what it declares. Nothing that the suites or the model program run imports `Library/GeneratorLibrary.fss` either. Before you cite a declaration as the library's way, check that a running program can reach it.
9	
10	## How loops and reductions call the library
11	
12	The desugarer, which both paths share, turns these forms into calls of the library:
13	
14	- `for x <- g do b end` becomes `g.loop(fn x => b)`, a call of the generator's `loop` method. Each further generator nests one more `loop` call inside.
15	- `while x <- e do b end` becomes `while __whileCond(e, fn x => b) do end`. `if x <- e then ... end` becomes a call of `__cond`.
16	- A comprehension or a big operator, such as `SUM`, becomes a call of `__bigOperator`, whose argument calls `__generate` on each generator. So does a big operator inside another: no desugaring calls the library's `__bigOperator2`.
17	
18	These functions work on the library's generators and reductions: `trait Generator` and `trait Reduction` in `FortressLibrary.fsi`, and `RangeInternals.fss` for ranges. `FortressLibrary.fss` also defines `__loop`, but no desugaring calls it. So a failure inside a loop or a reduction is most often in the library's code, and its fix is a library edit.
19	
20	## The curator's decisions on the library
21	
22	- Scalar ranges are over `ZZ32` only. A range over another integer type is a static error, and walk stops when it builds one. Write a wider counter as a `ZZ32` loop that widens its index.
23	- `ZZ32` and numerals convert into `RR64` implicitly. `ZZ64` converts into `RR64` only explicitly, by `asFloat`.
24	- For arithmetic that wraps on overflow, use the wrapping operators ∔ `DOTPLUS`, ∸ `DOTMINUS` and ⨰ `DOTTIMES`. Parenthesise every such expression fully, because their precedence is stated only among themselves.
25	- `SUM` and `PROD` are generic over `AdditiveGroup` and `MultiplicativeRing`. Write the element type wherever generators stand in brackets, also where the generators, the body or a declared type fix it: `SUM[\ZZ32\][j <- 0#n] f(j)`. The checker refuses a call without it (ledger row 731). Walk runs such a call at its value's declared type, or else at the join of its elements' run-time types. An empty `SUM` with no static argument written and no declared type gives the integer 0, and an empty `PROD` the integer 1, whatever the body's type (ledger row 716). With a static argument written that is not a number type, such as a user group, an empty or filtered `SUM` ends in `CastError` (ledger row 436).
26	- An indexed type's index parameter is bounded by `Index` (`revival-changes.md`, "Traits and objects"). `BoundedRange[\I\]` cannot take the bound, because the open range `(:)` stays a range over `Any` (P-56). So its `atMost(n: I): FullRange[\I\]` has the condition `where { I extends Index }`, which each call must meet (`Library/FortressLibrary.fsi`). A type whose static parameter is a range's index type takes the bound too, as `UniformDistribution[\T extends Index\]` over a `FullRange[\T\]` (`Library/Random.fsi`).
27	- An array's `fill` takes a value, and its `tabulate` a function of the index: `array[\ZZ32\](4).fill(0)`, `array[\ZZ32\](4).tabulate(fn (i:ZZ32):ZZ32 => 10 i)`. The factories that take a function are `tabulatedArray1` to `tabulatedArray3` and `tabulatedVector`.
28	
29	## Designing a change
30	
31	- Put each extension into this library, outside the compiler's files. This includes an extension that only the model program needs.
32	- Fix a gap in the library, not by a workaround in the program that meets it. Take the design from the library's practice as well as from the specification's text. If the two disagree, do as `specification.md`, "When the text and an implementation disagree", says.
33	- If a rule of the language or the checker refuses the way that you want, find how the library writes that kind of thing. Do the same. The checker's refusals of this library reach you through your brief, or through a run of the count stage (`compiler.md`): `fortress typecheck` checks against the compiler's prelude.
34	- When you add a method, make it dotted or functional as its family in the library does. If the family shows no practice, follow the team's proposal, which no program can import (`Library/incomplete/Collection.fss`): an updater, a getter or a setter, indexing included, is dotted, and every other method is functional.
35	- A new functional method reserves its name in every program that imports the library. The phase that binds names then refuses each program that names a variable or a parameter after it: "Variable even is already declared."
36	- A `fail` without a static argument has the result type `Any`. Where it must have a type, write the static argument, as `strToInt` calls `fail[\ZZ32\]`.
37	- A dotted method shadows a top-level function of the same name (`overloading.tex`, "Principles of Overloading").
38	- A new overload can make walk refuse every program at load. `interpreter.md`, "What walk checks", lists what walk refuses.
39	- A new native is a Java class under `interpreter/glue/prim/` (`interpreter.md`, "Natives"), so it is an edit of walk's Java too.
40	- `interpreter.md`, "The model program", says how to check microGPT under walk.
41	
42	## Editing
43	
44	A comment after a declaration that ends in an expression or a type becomes part of that declaration's source span. It also becomes part of the unambiguous name made from the span. So a comment-only edit changes the syntax tree. Before you compare parse trees or diagnostics across such an edit, map their positions back to the lines before the edit. Three removed scripts did this: `parse-compare.sh`, `ast-compare.py` and `remap-lines.py`. Print one with `git show ab067d9b6^:explorations/compile-ladder/rung-library-comments/<name>`.
45

1	# The specification
2	
3	Three folders hold the team's specification:
4	
5	- `Specification/` is the team's text, as the revival revises it. It says what the language means, except where a decision of the curator says otherwise.
6	- `Specification-1.0-frozen/` is the unrevised copy. Cite it as "the Working Draft of February 2011". Only `fortress.1.0.pdf` in it is the 1.0 release. Leave this copy unchanged.
7	- `Documentation/Specification/` is the team's later restart, which they did not finish. If its Types chapter, `Documentation/Specification/Prose/Language/types.tick`, covers a topic, cite it beside `Specification/` as the designers' later word.
8	
9	Appendix I, `Specification/appendices/changes.tex`, records the changes to the text. Its revival section has one entry for each change that the revival made.
10	
11	A draft build prints the team's `\note{}` boxes, and a release build hides them. Many say that a feature was not built, for example "Reduction variables are not yet supported." Before you record a missing feature as a gap, grep the notes of its chapter: `grep -n '\\note{' Specification/<file>.tex`.
12	
13	The api listings of the library part are generated from the library's `.fsi` files when the specification is built (`Specification/library/apis/`, not in the tree). A listing shows the library itself, so it cannot justify a change of the library. Cite the `.fsi` file.
14	
15	To weigh the specification against the team's later texts, or to find the designers' reason for a rule, read `exploring.md`, "Weighing the sources".
16	
17	## Changing the text: the revision form
18	
19	Every change of the text has the four parts below, so that no disagreement between the text and an implementation stays hidden.
20	
21	1. An entry in the revival section of Appendix I: a `\subsection` with a `\seclabel`. The entry gives:
22	   - the affected sections, the change, its rationale and its effect. The effect names each departure: each way in which walk or the compiled path does not do what the new text says, with its ledger row.
23	   - the original text, quoted with its path and line in `Specification-1.0-frozen/`;
24	   - what a reversal to the alternative not taken would need;
25	   - the decision of the curator that it follows (its POSITIONS entry), or the reason that your brief gives.
26	
27	   For the form, print one entry, about 2 KB: `explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'doc:Specification/appendices/changes.tex#choice of a coercion'`.
28	
29	2. At each changed passage, a callout that prints in every build, unlike a `\note`:
30	
31	       \revision{<label>}{<what changed, in a sentence or two>}
32	
33	   `<label>` is the `\seclabel` of the entry. `Specification/fortress/fortress.tex` defines `\revision`.
34	
35	3. The front matter's one paragraph on the revision, in `Specification/fortress/preamble.tex`. If your change makes it false, correct it.
36	
37	4. The full reasoning, in `decision-record.md` in the folder of your work under `explorations/`: each changed passage, the original and the new text, the reason, and the way back. For the form, print one passage of an earlier record, about 4 KB: `explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'doc:explorations/compile-ladder/rung-spec-route-a/decision-record.md#3.3'`.
38	
39	If the revision refuses an example, keep the example in the text, marked "Not allowed", as the specification itself does. If your change contradicts a calculus of Appendix A, keep the calculus's rules and soundness claims. Add a callout to it that says what it predates.
40	
41	Check each changed sentence of `Specification/` or `Documentation/` against the curator's decisions. If it says what walk or the compiled path does, run a program that shows it.
42	
43	## Building it
44	
45	To check your LaTeX, build the specification in a built tree, after the setup lines. It takes about 90 s, so start it detached (`session.md`, "Long commands"):
46	
47	    nohup bash -c '( cd Specification/fortress && ./ant genSource && ./ant tex ) > tmp/spec.txt 2>&1; echo EXIT=$? >> tmp/spec.txt' >/dev/null 2>&1 &
48	
49	- Both commands must end in `BUILD SUCCESSFUL`, and `grep -c 'Reference .* undefined\|multiply defined\|Undefined control sequence' Specification/fortress/fortress.log` must print 0.
50	- If `pdflatex` is missing, install the packages of the `PKGS` line of `explorations/experiment/setup.sh` with `apt-get update -qq && apt-get install -y`.
51	- The build writes only ignored files, its log among them, which can reach 400 MB. Remove them afterwards: `git clean -fXq -- Specification`.

54	## When the text and an implementation disagree
55	
56	- If a decision of the curator says which side is correct, the other side is wrong. If the wrong side is in your area, change it to agree. If not, record the departure as `tests-writing.md`, "How a defect is recorded", says.
57	- If no decision says so, the disagreement is a conflict. Switch to exploring (`exploring.md`).
58	- If the passage has an Appendix I entry, name the departure or the conflict in the entry's effect, with its ledger row. Then the text claims no more than holds.
59	
60	## Citing it
61	
62	- If your change renames or removes a section that a test names, update that citation in the same commit.
63	- Inside the text, cite a section with `\secref{label}`.
64

1	# The gate
2	
3	The gate runs the seven steps below on one tree, in about 25 minutes. It is green if every step passes, and red if one fails. If a step fails, run the rest, so that the summary holds every step's result.
4	
5	## What it writes
6	
7	The summary, `summary.txt`, has one tab-separated row for each suite: `track/suite`, tests, failures, errors, skipped. Below the rows, lines that start with `#` give each log's `BUILD` and `Total time:` lines, the machine that ran the gate (`# machine`), the atomic runs and the ladder's comparison. A landed summary can also end with `# microgpt-walk` lines: the `VERDICT:` and `rc=` lines of the microGPT walk check (`interpreter.md`, "The model program"), run on the landed tree. Add them only if your brief asks for the microGPT walk check on the landed tree.
8	
9	If your brief asks you to land a gate's results, put them in a new `gate/` folder in `explorations/compile-ladder/`, under the `climb-batch-` name that your brief gives, in the form of the newest one: `summary.txt`, and in `ladder/` the files `ladder.tsv`, `microgpt-phase.md`, `comparison.txt` and `microgpt-comparison.txt`. The next gate compares with the newest summary there or in `explorations/compile-ladder/gate-baseline/`, and finds no other. Land them in a commit that changes nothing else that the gate reads.
10	
11	Steps 5 and 7 use shell functions that `explorations/coordinator/tools/gate-functions.sh` defines. The file runs nothing. In each Bash call of steps 5 and 7, set up the call as `build-and-caches.md` says, which sets `FORTRESS_HOME` to the tree's root. Then source the file, from the root:
12	
13	    source explorations/coordinator/tools/gate-functions.sh
14	
15	## When to run it
16	
17	Your brief says whether you run the gate. If it does not ask, run only your own tests (`tests-running.md`).
18	
19	If it asks, first check whether the newest gate still holds for your tree. A gate's tables stay valid until the tree changes under `ProjectFortress/` or `Library/`, or in `build.xml`, outside the test files. A test file is a `.fss`, `.fsi` or `.test` file directly in `ProjectFortress/tests/` or a `ProjectFortress/*_tests/` directory. The commit that landed the newest summary changed nothing that the gate reads. Commit your tree, then run this command. It prints each path, test files excepted, changed since that commit:
20	
21	    G=$(git log -1 --format=%H -- 'explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-*/gate/summary.txt')
22	    git diff --name-only $G HEAD -- ProjectFortress Library build.xml \
23	        | grep -v -E '^ProjectFortress/([^/]*_)?tests/[^/]*\.(fss|fsi|test)$'
24	
25	- If it prints a path, run the gate.
26	- If not, the newest gate holds. Run only the changed test files, through `harness-one.sh` and `junit.sh` (`tests-running.md`).
27	
28	## The steps
29	
30	Run these steps from the tree's root. Keep the logs of steps 2 and 4 in `tmp/gate/`, as `compileAll.txt`, `testFast.txt`, `testSystem.txt` and `testSpecData.txt`.
31	
32	1. Read the Avail column of `df -h /`. Warning: deleting `/tmp/fortress*rats` can break other live runs. If the column shows less than 1 GB, delete `/tmp/fortress*rats`, `ProjectFortress/test-tmp` and `ProjectFortress/test-caches`, and read it again. If it still shows less than 500 MB, stop and report.
33	2. Run `rm -rf ProjectFortress/TEST-RESULTS tmp/gate && mkdir -p tmp/gate`, then `ant compileAll`.
34	3. If the build printed `Caches <tree>/default_repository/caches started again, empty`, run the library order (`build-and-caches.md`). If not, and a source of the compiler's library changed since the caches were filled, take its step in `build-and-caches.md`, "After an edit of the library". Then copy the caches twice for the ladder regression, before anything else compiles into them:
35	
36	       D=$PWD/tmp/gate/ladder ; mkdir -p $D/root
37	       cp -a default_repository/caches $D/root/ladder-caches
38	       cp -a default_repository/caches $D/root/pristine
39	
40	4. Run `ant testFast`, then `ant testSystem`, then `ant testSpecData`. All three must have zero failures.
41	5. Write the summary: `gate_summary tmp/gate tmp/gate/summary.txt`. Compare it: `gate_compare "$(last_landed_summary)" tmp/gate/summary.txt`. It prints a line for a suite with failures or errors, a suite with no tests, a suite whose count of tests fell, and a suite that is gone. Each such line makes the gate red. A count that rose prints nothing.
42	6. Do the atomic runs, and append their lines to the summary.
43	7. Do the ladder regression.
44	
45	## The atomic runs
46	
47	The atomic runs compile fourteen programs, and run each one three times at four threads, in about a minute. They need the library's jars in the tree's caches (`build-and-caches.md`). Run them from `ProjectFortress/`:
48	
49	    for p in AtomicTopLevelObjectVar AtomicTopLevelVar MutableTopLevelVarInLoop FirstLoadThreadsRungG \
50	             atomic0 atomic1 atomic2 atomic3 atomic4 atomic5 atomic6 \
51	             nestedTransactions0 nestedTransactions1 nestedTransactions2 ; do
52	      d=other_compiler_tests ; [ -f compiler_tests/$p.fss ] && d=compiler_tests
53	      timeout -k 5 300 ../bin/fortress compile $d/$p.fss >/dev/null 2>&1 || { echo "# atomic $p COMPILE-FAILED" ; continue ; }
54	      for i in 1 2 3 ; do
55	        out=$(FORTRESS_THREADS=4 timeout -k 5 120 ../bin/fortress run $p 2>&1) ; rc=$?
56	        [ $rc -eq 124 ] && { out=$(FORTRESS_THREADS=4 timeout -k 5 120 ../bin/fortress run $p 2>&1) ; rc=$? ; }
57	        case "$out" in *FAIL*) r=FAIL ;; *PASS*) r=PASS ;; *) r="NO-PASS rc=$rc" ;; esac
58	        [ $rc -eq 124 ] && r=TIMEOUT-TWICE
59	        echo "# atomic $p run$i threads=4 $r"
60	      done
61	    done
62	
63	The gate is red on any FAIL, NO-PASS, COMPILE-FAILED or TIMEOUT-TWICE.
64	
65	## The ladder regression
66	
67	The compile ladder records how far each test program gets through the compiler's phases, in order: parse, disambiguate, typecheck, codegen, link, run and pass. The ladder regression runs part of it again, and compares the result with the baseline, `explorations/compile-ladder/baseline-2026-09-19/`:
68	
69	- It compiles and runs the 85 programs of the baseline's `pass-list.txt`. It compares each one's phase and output with the baseline's `raw/`.
70	- It compiles the eighteen components of the two microGPT programs, and never runs them. It compares each one's phase with the baseline's `microgpt-phase.md`.
71	
72	A file that moved gets a mark:
73	
74	- DOWN: a phase lower than the record.
75	- MISSING: a file with no output.
76	- STDOUT: output that differs from the record after the `Operation took <n>ms` line is masked.
77	- UP: a phase higher than the record. This is progress, not red.
78	
79	DOWN, MISSING and STDOUT are red, unless your brief declared that move as expected before the gate ran.
80	Warning: do not run `run-ladder.sh`, the driver over every test program, with its defaults. Its default root is shared, its cache pruning corrupts a parallel run, and its default `OUT` is a tracked folder.
81	
82	To run it, as step 7, with step 3's copies of the caches:
83	
84	1. Copy the drivers into `tmp/gate/ladder/`, and point their outputs and caches there:
85	
86	       D=$PWD/tmp/gate/ladder ; B=explorations/compile-ladder/baseline-2026-09-19
87	       cp explorations/compile-ladder/repair-r1-atomic-static/run-subset.sh \
88	          $B/classify.py $B/microgpt-phase.sh $B/microgpt-phase.py $D/
89	       sed -i -e "s|^OUT=.*|OUT=$D|" -e "s|^LADDER_ROOT=.*|LADDER_ROOT=$D/root|" $D/run-subset.sh
90	       sed -i -e "s|/home/user/fortress|$PWD|g" \
91	           -e "s|^export LADDER_CACHES=.*|export LADDER_CACHES=$D/root/ladder-caches|" \
92	           -e "s|^export LADDER_TMP=.*|export LADDER_TMP=$D/root/ladder-tmp|" \
93	           -e "s|^RAW=.*|RAW=$D/raw/microgpt|" -e "s|^TSV=.*|TSV=$D/microgpt-results.tsv|" $D/microgpt-phase.sh
94	       tail -n +2 $B/pass-list.txt | cut -f1 | sed 's|/|\t|' > $D/subset.txt
95	
96	2. Run the four scripts, with no arguments, in this order: `bash $D/run-subset.sh`, `python3 $D/classify.py`, `bash $D/microgpt-phase.sh` and `python3 $D/microgpt-phase.py`. Each reads and writes in `$D`. This takes about 200 s for the 85 and 35 s for the eighteen, so run them in the background (`session.md`, "Long commands"). With step 3's copies, the driver skips the library's build (about 145 s).
97	3. Compare: `ladder_compare $B $D`, then `diff <(mg_phases $B/microgpt-phase.md) <(mg_phases $D/microgpt-phase.md)`. Append each line that they print to the summary, with `# ladder ` before it.
98	
99	If your brief asks for your change's own ladder subset, write your own `subset.txt`. Put in it each file whose recorded first error in the baseline's `raw/` names something that your change touched. Run them after your edit only. Compare them with the newest landed `ladder.tsv`, or with the baseline's `raw/` for a file that the gate does not run.
100	
101	## Comparing with an earlier run
102	
103	- `ant testSystem` runs in four shards, the summary's rows `system-0` to `system-3`. A shard takes the files by their place in a sorted list, so an added file moves every later file to another shard. When you compare by hand, compare only the sum of the four. `gate_compare` sums them.
104	- In printed output, mask only these differences: the `Operation took <n>ms` line, a Java line number in a stack frame, an object's identity hash (`@` and hex digits), and a position in a library file that your change moved. In your report, list each test with a masked difference, and the kinds masked in it.
105	- If your brief asks you to compare the interpreter tests with a base run, use the two scripts in `explorations/coordinator/tools/count-run/`. `count-run.sh` runs every `ProjectFortress/tests/*.fss` under walk, one JVM per test: run it once on the base commit and once after your edit. `compare-normalised.py` compares the two runs, with the last three masks above. Each script's header gives its usage.
106

1	# Committing and pushing
2	
3	**scratch**
4	: Files and folders that your work makes and `main` does not keep: logs, captured and raw run output, copies of tools, probe programs, lists and private caches folders.
5	
6	Your brief says whether you commit and push, and on which branch. If it says nothing, commit on your current branch, and push it.
7	
8	## What to commit
9	
10	- Commit your change, its tests, your report if it is a file, and any reusable script.
11	- Commit what you write to the record, such as a ledger row, with the work that it records. A row's close follows the fix's commit (`records.md`).
12	- Keep scratch in your tree's `tmp/`, which is gitignored.
13	- In a fresh clone, `.claude/worktrees/` and `.claude/agents/` show as untracked, because the lines of `.git/info/exclude` that hide them are not in the clone. Do not commit them.
14	- Keep a copyrighted PDF or deck in `research/decks/`, which is gitignored. Cite it by its Wayback URL. Notes on it go in `research/extracts/`: your own summary, with brief attributed quotations.
15	- Put provenance and rationale in commit messages and reports, not in source comments.
16	- Name a model by its tier (Opus, Sonnet, Fable) in any text that you commit, commit messages included. Never write its model identifier, the API's name for the model, which starts with `claude-`.
17	
18	## How to commit
19	
20	Commit as you go, each commit in one command that names its paths:
21	
22	    git add -- <paths> && git commit -m "<message>" -- <paths>
23	
24	- The command commits only the paths that it names. Other agents may have uncommitted edits in your tree. Leave them alone.
25	- If you renamed a file with `git mv`, name its old path in `git commit` only, because `git add` refuses a path that no longer exists: `git add -- <new paths> && git commit -m "<message>" -- <new paths> <old paths>`.
26	- Never commit a copied directory, and never use `git add -A`.
27	- Before you commit more than a few hundred lines, stage them and read what you staged: `git add -- <paths> && git diff --cached --stat -- <paths>`.
28	- If the commit edits the original tree, say so in its message.
29	- End every commit message with this footer, exactly, whatever footer Claude Code suggests:
30	
31	      Co-Authored-By: Claude <noreply@anthropic.com>
32	      Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01AmiXNpJxQ6TBwec4vJZHDB
33	
34	  If your brief gives another session line, use it.
35	
36	## Pushing
37	
38	Push after every commit, so that a lost container loses nothing.
39	
40	- If you work on your own branch, push it: `git push -u origin <branch>` the first time, then `git push`. Your brief says how the branch reaches `main`.
41	- If you work on `main`, other agents commit to it too. Push only your own commits:
42	  1. Run `git log origin/main..main`. Your commits are those whose hashes your own `git commit` printed.
43	  2. If it lists another agent's commit, run the command again shortly: that agent pushes right after it commits. If the commit stays, push nothing, and say so in your report.
44	  3. If it lists only your commits, push three times, in this order:
45	
46	         git push origin main
47	         git push origin main:claude/worker-brief-fable-vnnuv8
48	         git push origin main:blinded-fable
49	
50	     The third push keeps `blinded-fable` current. If the container is lost, the platform rebuilds it from that branch.
51	- Push no branch that this section does not name, unless your brief names it.
52	- If a push is refused, push nothing more, and say so in your report.

A trait or object that extends a type under a `where` condition is that type only where the condition holds, and its members are checked with the condition holding (conditional extension). A `where` condition on a function's or a method's own static parameters bounds them. 39	- P-45 **Overloaded declarations may differ in their static parameters.** The specification drops its sentence that forbids this, and keeps it as superseded text. It states instead the overloading model of the type group's 2011 paper (`Papers/Types/`), which the compiled checker already used. The checker keeps the paper's three rules: No Duplicates, Meet and Return Type. It checks the Return Type Rule over every instance of a generic declaration that the argument types allow, not over one guessed instance. One rule of the old sentence survives: if one generic declaration is more specific than another, their static parameters must line up position by position, as Java's rule for overriding a generic method requires. The compiled checker tests it only where the two declarations have as many static parameters of their own (F-75). Walk chooses among overloads by the parameter types that each declaration declares, not by the order in which they are written. At load, walk judges each pair of two generic declarations by the checker's rules on their declared parameter types. It does not refuse a pair only because none of their parameter types exclude, as when one declaration is more specific than the other. Walk and the checker must accept the same pairs. The library repairs, by declarations of its own, the overload sets that the checker refused, and no line of microGPT's two programs changes. 9	### The words this record uses
10	
11	- **Walk** is the interpreter. It runs a program without static types. The **compiled path** checks a program's types with the **checker**, then makes JVM bytecode. 13	- **The full check** is the checker's overloading check reading the symbolic operators too (`+`, `-`, `=`, `||`, the subscripts `[ ]` and the rest). Today it reads only operators named by a word of capitals, such as `MAX` (row 584); P-155 turns it on. The **shadow** is a copy of the checker with the full check on, compiled beside the build; the symbolic-operator probe measured with it.
14	- An **api** is a component's interface (a `.fsi` file); the **component** is its code (a `.fss` file). The **export error** is one error that lists every declaration where an api and its component differ; each declaration it lists is an **entry**.
15	- A **tuple** is a value such as `(1, 2)`. An array of rank 2 is indexed by a pair: `m[i, j]` passes the pair `(i, j)`.
16	- A **row** is an entry of the gap ledger, cited by number. An **item** is a numbered question in PLAN's list "Pavol's answers".
17	- A **rung** is one fix, built by one worker in its own copy of the tree and checked by a second worker, the skeptic. A **batch** is a few rungs, merged and tested together by the **gate** and landed at once. **Two runs of one record** are two batches, the second launched after the first lands, as batches 6 and 6b and 7 and 7b ran.
18	- **Test first.** Every fix starts with a test that shows the defect, seen failing before the edit and passing after. An **expected failure** is a test named `XXX...` that passes while the defect is there; when the fix lands it is **promoted** to a plain name. A **guard** is a test that passes before and after.

558	The batch runs on the workflow of batch 20: `coordinator/climb-batch-workflow.js`, its manual `coordinator/climb-batch-workflow.md`, and the practice they build, `coordinator/process-engineering/batch-redesign.md`. Each rung's worker does its rung test first; its skeptic checks it and fixes what it finds, test first; a judge rules only on a fix the skeptic marks contested, on a rung the skeptic refuses, or on a worker's stop; the gather lands the rungs on `main` and folds their record lines and their ledger rows through `coordinator/tools/ledger.py`; the merged-diff review and the gate run side by side; the commit stage lands the gate's tables, runs the quick microGPT walk check and pushes. The batch writes no skill text. Section 3 is each worker's brief word for word; this section holds the rest of the manifest, which `explorations/compile-ladder/plan-21/manifest/gen21.py` reads with the briefings of `lists21.py` beside it, and `check21.js` checks.

entries.name: TaskCreate
entries.description:
Use this tool to create a structured task list for your current coding session. This helps you track progress, organize complex tasks, and demonstrate thoroughness to the user.
It also helps the user understand the progress of the task and overall progress of their requests.

## When to Use This Tool

Use this tool proactively in these scenarios:

- Complex multi-step tasks - When a task requires 3 or more distinct steps or actions
- Non-trivial and complex tasks - Tasks that require careful planning or multiple operations
- Plan mode - When using plan mode, create a task list to track the work
- User explicitly requests todo list - When the user directly asks you to use the todo list
- User provides multiple tasks - When users provide a list of things to be done (numbered or comma-separated)
- After receiving new instructions - Immediately capture user requirements as tasks
- When you start working on a task - Mark it as in_progress BEFORE beginning work
- After completing a task - Mark it as completed and add any new follow-up tasks discovered during implementation

## When NOT to Use This Tool

Skip using this tool when:
- There is only a single, straightforward task
- The task is trivial and tracking it provides no organizational benefit
- The task can be completed in less than 3 trivial steps
- The task is purely conversational or informational

NOTE that you should not use this tool if there is only one trivial task to do. In this case you are better off just doing the task directly.

## Task Fields

- **subject**: A brief, actionable title in imperative form (e.g., "Fix authentication bug in login flow")
- **description**: What needs to be done
- **activeForm** (optional): Present continuous form shown in the spinner when the task is in_progress (e.g., "Fixing authentication bug"). If omitted, the spinner shows the subject instead.

All tasks are created with status `pending`.

## Tips

- Create tasks with clear, specific subjects that describe the outcome
- After creating tasks, use TaskUpdate to set up dependencies (blocks/blockedBy) if needed
- Check TaskList first to avoid creating duplicate tasks

subject.description: A brief title for the task

activeForm.description: Present continuous form shown in spinner when in_progress (e.g., "Running tests")

metadata.description: Arbitrary metadata to attach to the task

entries.name: TaskList
entries.description:
Use this tool to list all tasks in the task list.

## When to Use This Tool

- To see what tasks are available to work on (status: 'pending', no owner, not blocked)
- To check overall progress on the project
- To find tasks that are blocked and need dependencies resolved
- After completing a task, to check for newly unblocked work or claim the next available task
- **Prefer working on tasks in ID order** (lowest ID first) when multiple tasks are available, as earlier tasks often set up context for later ones

## Output

Returns a summary of each task:
- **id**: Task identifier (use with TaskGet, TaskUpdate)
- **subject**: Brief description of the task
- **status**: 'pending', 'in_progress', or 'completed'
- **owner**: Agent ID if assigned, empty if available
- **blockedBy**: List of open task IDs that must be resolved first (tasks with blockedBy cannot be claimed until dependencies resolve)

Use TaskGet with a specific task ID to view full details including description and comments.

entries.name: TaskUpdate
entries.description:
Use this tool to update a task in the task list.

## When to Use This Tool

**Mark tasks as resolved:**
- When you have completed the work described in a task
- When a task is no longer needed or has been superseded
- IMPORTANT: Always mark your assigned tasks as resolved when you finish them
- After resolving, call TaskList to find your next task

- ONLY mark a task as completed when you have FULLY accomplished it
- If you encounter errors, blockers, or cannot finish, keep the task as in_progress
- When blocked, create a new task describing what needs to be resolved
- Never mark a task as completed if:
  - Tests are failing
  - Implementation is partial
  - You encountered unresolved errors
  - You couldn't find necessary files or dependencies

**Delete tasks:**
- When a task is no longer relevant or was created in error
- Setting status to `deleted` permanently removes the task

**Update task details:**
- When requirements change or become clearer
- When establishing dependencies between tasks

## Fields You Can Update

- **status**: The task status (see Status Workflow below)
- **subject**: Change the task title (imperative form, e.g., "Run tests")
- **description**: Change the task description
- **activeForm**: Present continuous form shown in spinner when in_progress (e.g., "Running tests")
- **owner**: Change the task owner (agent name)
- **metadata**: Merge metadata keys into the task (set a key to null to delete it)
- **addBlocks**: Mark tasks that cannot start until this one completes
- **addBlockedBy**: Mark tasks that must complete before this one can start

## Status Workflow

Status progresses: `pending` → `in_progress` → `completed`

Use `deleted` to permanently remove a task.

## Staleness

Make sure to read a task's latest state using `TaskGet` before updating it.

## Examples

Mark task as in progress when starting work:
```json
{"taskId": "1", "status": "in_progress"}
```

Mark task as completed after finishing work:
```json
{"taskId": "1", "status": "completed"}
```

Delete a task:
```json
{"taskId": "1", "status": "deleted"}
```

Claim a task by setting owner:
```json
{"taskId": "1", "owner": "my-name"}
```

Set up task dependencies:
```json
{"taskId": "2", "addBlockedBy": ["1"]}
```

taskId.description: The ID of the task to update

activeForm.description: Present continuous form shown in spinner when in_progress (e.g., "Running tests")

addBlocks.description: Task IDs that this task blocks

addBlockedBy.description: Task IDs that block this task

metadata.description: Metadata keys to merge into the task. Set a key to null to delete it.

count[\E\](b: Box[\E\]): ZZ32 = 1

run(): () = do

132					       f.getReturnType.unwrap, getStaticParameters(f, true))),
133			           if (isFunctionalMethod(f))
134				     Some(f.asInstanceOf[JavaFunctionalMethod].selfPosition)
135				   else None,
136				   Some(f)))
137	      def isAbstract(a: (ArrowType,Option[Int],Option[JavaFunctional])) =

139	      if (!onlyConcrete || !arrows.exists(isAbstract)) return arrows

143	      def declarer(f: JavaFunctional): Option[TypeConsIndex] =

196	    private def paramsWithoutSelf(d: (JavaFunctional, StaticTypeReplacer, TraitType)): Option[Type] = d match {

211	         .toList.map(p => p match { case (f, replacer, _) =>
212	              val (sparams, apart) = ownStaticParamsApart(f)
213	              (NF.makeArrowType(f.getSpan,
214		                        replacer.replaceIn(apart(paramsToType(f.asInstanceOf[JavaMethod].selfType.unwrap, f.parameters, f.getSpan))),

221	     * of the trait or object being checked renamed apart, so that the arguments the
222	     * replacer puts in place of the declaring trait's parameters are not captured. */
223	    private def ownStaticParamsApart(f: JavaFunctional): (JavaList[StaticParam], Type => Type) = {
224	      val own = toListFromImmutable(getStaticParameters(f, false))
225	      val env = typeAnalyzer.env
226	      val taken = own.map(_.getName.getText).toSet
227	      val clash = own.filter(p => env.contains(p.getName))
228	      if (clash.isEmpty) return (getStaticParameters(f, false), (t: Type) => t)
229	      val subst: List[(IdOrOp, IdOrOp)] = clash.map { p =>
230	        val n = p.getName
231	        val fresh = Iterator.from(1).map(i => NF.makeId(NU.getSpan(n), n.getText + "$" + i))
232	                            .find(m => !env.contains(m) && !taken.contains(m.getText)).get
233	        (n, fresh) }
234	      def apart(t: Type): Type = alphaRename(subst, t).asInstanceOf[Type]
235	      // every own parameter's bounds are renamed, so that a bound naming a renamed parameter names it still
236	      val renamed = own.map(p => {
237	        def bounds = toJavaList(toListFromImmutable(p.getExtendsClause).map(b => alphaRename(subst, b).asInstanceOf[BaseType]))
238	        subst.find(_._1 == p.getName) match {
239	          case Some((_, m)) => NF.makeStaticParam(p, m.asInstanceOf[Id], bounds)
240	          case None => p.getName match {
241	            case n: Id if !p.getExtendsClause.isEmpty => NF.makeStaticParam(p, n, bounds)
242	            case _ => p }
243	        } })
244	      (toJavaList(renamed), apart)
245	    }

547	    /* A pair's validity depends on its two signatures as instantiated where it is checked,

552	    /* The exclusion test alone reads the self of a trait whose self type comes from its
553	     * F-bound as the trait met with that self type, C[\X\] & X, which every extender is,
554	     * since it must be a subtype of the static argument that it gives. For a functional
555	     * method of such a trait, parameters() keeps self at the plain trait type, which
556	     * specificity, the Meet Rule, the coverage rule and the Return Type Rule read; the
557	     * declaration's own parameters (FunctionalMethod.ast) keep its TraitSelfType. An arrow
558	     * made from those by the same steps as the plain arrow is kept beside it, keyed by the
559	     * plain arrow's identity, and validOverloadingInner's exclusion test reads it. */
560	    private val exclusionArrows = new java.util.IdentityHashMap[ArrowType, ArrowType]()
561	    private def selfTyped(a: ArrowType, f: JavaFunctional, mk: JavaList[Param] => ArrowType): ArrowType = {

577	    private def validOverloading(first: (ArrowType,Option[Int],Option[JavaFunctional]),
578					 second: (ArrowType,Option[Int],Option[JavaFunctional]),
579					 signatures: List[(ArrowType,Option[Int],Option[JavaFunctional])],
580					 isMethod: Boolean,

583	        val fnal1 = first._3
584	        val fnal2 = second._3
585	        if (cacheOverloadChecks && !fnal1.isEmpty && !fnal2.isEmpty) {

587	                       signatures.map(s => (s._1, s._2)).toSet, isMethod, staticParamsInScope)
588	            val cv = validOverloadingMemo.get(key)
589	            if (!cv.isEmpty && cv.get)

599	    /* Checks the overloading rules: subtype / exclusion / meet */
600	    private def validOverloadingInner(first: (ArrowType,Option[Int],Option[JavaFunctional]),
601					      second: (ArrowType,Option[Int],Option[JavaFunctional]),
602					      signatures: List[(ArrowType,Option[Int],Option[JavaFunctional])],
603					      isMethod: Boolean,

605					      debug:Boolean=false): Boolean = {
606	      val (fa, fsp, _) = first
607	      val (ga, gsp, _) = second
608	      true
609	      
610	      if (oa.lteq(fa, ga)) { true }
611	      else if (oa.lteq(ga, fa)) { true }
612	      else if (functionalMethodsAtOnePosition(first, second, isMethod)) { true }
613	      else if (meetRule(first, second, signatures, isMethod, oa, debug)) { true }
614	      else if (oa.excludes(forExclusion(fa), forExclusion(ga))) { true }
615	      else { coverageRule(first, second, signatures, isMethod, oa) }
616	    
617	      
618	  /*    
619	      println("Specificity\n")
620	      val b1 = oa.lteq(fa, ga)
621	      if (b1) true 
622	      val b2 = oa.lteq(ga, fa) 
623	      if (b2) return true
624	      println("Meet Rule\n")
625	      val b3 = meetRule(first, second, signatures, isMethod, oa, debug)
626	      if (b3) return true
627	      println("Exclusion\n")
628	      val b4 = oa.excludes(fa, ga) 
629	      println("Done")
630	      return b4
631	  */
632	
633	      //if (b1) !b2 else ( b2 || b3 || b4 )  //JT: It looks like the duplicate rule IS enforced somewhere else
634	      //(b1 || b2 || b3 || b4)
635	    }
636	
637	    /* The Meet Rule for Functional Methods: two functional methods with their self
638	     * parameters at one position are a valid overloading among the top-level functionals;
639	     * the meet the rule asks of a trait or object that provides both is checked for that
640	     * trait or object (checkOverloading's loop over them). */
641	    private def functionalMethodsAtOnePosition(first: (ArrowType,Option[Int],Option[JavaFunctional]),
642	                                               second: (ArrowType,Option[Int],Option[JavaFunctional]),
643	                                               isMethod: Boolean): Boolean =
644	      !isMethod && first._2.isDefined && first._2 == second._2 &&
645	      first._3.exists(isFunctionalMethod) && second._3.exists(isFunctionalMethod)
646	
647	    private def meetRule(first: (ArrowType,Option[Int],Option[JavaFunctional]),
648	    	                 second: (ArrowType,Option[Int],Option[JavaFunctional]),
649				 signatures: List[(ArrowType,Option[Int],Option[JavaFunctional])],
650				 isMethod: Boolean,
651				 oa: OverloadingOracle,
652				 debug : Boolean = false): Boolean = {
653	      val (fa, fsp, _) = first
654	      val (ga, gsp, _) = second
655	      val b1 = fsp == gsp
656	      val b2 = (fsp == gsp) &&
657	      signatures.exists(third => third match {
658	           case (ha, hsp, _) => {
659	              val a1 = (hsp == fsp) 
660	              val a2 = a1 && oa.lteq(ha, fa) 
661	              val a3 = a2 && oa.lteq(ha, ga) 
662	              val a4 = a3 && (if (isMethod && fsp.isDefined)
663	                                oa.isMeet(withoutSelf(ha, fsp.get), withoutSelf(fa, fsp.get), withoutSelf(ga, fsp.get), false, debug)
664	                              else oa.isMeet(ha, fa, ga, isMethod, debug))
665	     //         if (debug)
666	     //             println("" + ha + " " + a1 + a2 + a3 + a4)
667	                   
668	              a4}})
669	      b2
670	    }
671	
672	    // the self parameter of a functional method is compared as a dotted method's receiver is, wherever it sits
673	    private def withoutSelf(a: ArrowType, i: Int): ArrowType = {
674	      val d = a.getDomain match {
675	        case t: TupleType =>
676	          NF.makeTupleType(NU.getSpan(t), toJavaList(toListFromImmutable(t.getElements).zipWithIndex.filter(_._2 != i).map(_._1)))
677	        case t => NF.makeTupleType(NU.getSpan(t), toJavaList(List[Type]()))
678	      }
679	      NF.makeArrowType(NU.getSpan(a), d, a.getRange, a.getInfo.getStaticParams)
680	    }
681	
682	    /* The Meet Rule's closed-trait case, for functions and functional methods: the
683	     * declarations whose domains are below both domains together hold every value of
684	     * their overlap, as the comprises clauses show (OverloadingOracle.coversOverlap).
685	     * For functional methods of a trait or object that provides them, the overlap is
686	     * read without the self parameter, as meetRule reads the meet. */
687	    private def coverageRule(first: (ArrowType,Option[Int],Option[JavaFunctional]),
688	                             second: (ArrowType,Option[Int],Option[JavaFunctional]),
689	                             signatures: List[(ArrowType,Option[Int],Option[JavaFunctional])],
690	                             isMethod: Boolean,
691	                             oa: OverloadingOracle): Boolean = {
692	      val (fa, fsp, _) = first
693	      val (ga, gsp, _) = second
694	      if (fsp != gsp || (isMethod && fsp.isEmpty)) false
695	      else {
696	        val hs = signatures.collect {
697	          case (ha, hsp, _) if hsp == fsp && !(ha eq fa) && !(ha eq ga) &&
698	                               oa.lteq(ha, fa) && oa.lteq(ha, ga) => ha }
699	        if (isMethod) {
700	          val i = fsp.get
701	          oa.coversOverlap(withoutSelf(fa, i), withoutSelf(ga, i), hs.map(withoutSelf(_, i)))
702	        }
703	        else oa.coversOverlap(fa, ga, hs)
704	      }
705	    }
706	
707	    /* The return types of a declaration o and of a declaration p that it keeps the type
708	     * declaring it from inheriting (STypesUtil.providedAndOverridden). Where their parameter
709	     * types are the same, the two are checked as the pair of an overloading was, o being the
710	     * more specific; where o has the modifier override and widens p's, o's return type must be
711	     * a subtype of p's (traits.tex, "Method Declarations"): with static parameters, at every
712	     * instance of p, and where both declare as many of their own, also position by position. */
713	    private def checkOverridingReturnType(name: IdOrOpOrAnonymousName,
714	                                          o: (JavaFunctional, StaticTypeReplacer, TraitType),
715	                                          p: (JavaFunctional, StaticTypeReplacer, TraitType),
716	                                          equal: Boolean,
717	                                          oracle: OverloadingOracle): Unit = {
718	      def arrow(d: (JavaFunctional, StaticTypeReplacer, TraitType)) =
719	        if (isFunctionalMethod(d._1)) toFunctionalMethodArrows(Set(d), oracle).headOption
720	        else toMethodArrows(Set(d)).headOption
721	      (arrow(o), arrow(p)) match {
722	        case (Some(oa), Some(pa)) =>
723	          if (equal) {
724	            returnTypeCheck(name, oa, pa, oracle)
725	            returnTypeCheck(name, pa, oa, oracle)
726	          } else {
727	            def own(a: ArrowType) = toListFromImmutable(a.getInfo.getStaticParams).filter(!_.isLifted)
728	            // the self parameter, or a dotted method's receiver, apart
729	            val at = oa._2.getOrElse(0)
730	            val holds =
731	              if (own(oa._1).isEmpty && own(pa._1).isEmpty)
732	                isTrue(typeAnalyzer.subtype(oa._1.getRange, pa._1.getRange))(typeAnalyzer)
733	              else oracle.sa.subtypeUA(withoutSelf(oa._1, at), withoutSelf(pa._1, at)) &&
734	                   oracle.satisfiesPositionalRule(oa._1, pa._1)
735	            if (!holds)
736	              error(mergeSpan(oa._1, pa._1),
737	                    "For " + name + ",\nthe return type of the overriding declaration " + typeAndSpanToString(oa._1) +
738	                    " should be a subtype of the\n    return type of the declaration it overrides " + typeAndSpanToString(pa._1))
739	          }
740	        case _ =>
741	      }
742	    }
743	
744	    private def returnTypeCheck(name: IdOrOpOrAnonymousName,
745	    	    			first: (ArrowType,Option[Int],Option[JavaFunctional]),
746	                                second: (ArrowType,Option[Int],Option[JavaFunctional]),
747				        oa: OverloadingOracle) = {
748	      val (fa, fsp, _) = first
749	      val (ga, gsp, _) = second
750	//          println("Satisfies return type rule?\n   " + typeAndSpanToString(fa) + "\n   " + typeAndSpanToString(ga))
751	      if (!oa.satisfiesReturnTypeRule(fa, ga)) {
752	//        println("For " + name + ",\nthe return type of " + typeAndSpanToString(fa) + " should be a subtype of the\n    return type of " + typeAndSpanToString(ga))
753	        error(mergeSpan(fa, ga),
754		      "For " + name + ",\nthe return type of " + typeAndSpanToString(fa) + " should be a subtype of the\n    return type of " + typeAndSpanToString(ga))
755	      }
756	      else if (oa.lteq(fa, ga) && !oa.satisfiesPositionalRule(fa, ga))
757	        error(mergeSpan(fa, ga),
758	              "For " + name + ",\nthe static parameters of " + typeAndSpanToString(fa) + " should correspond position by position\n    to those of " + typeAndSpanToString(ga) +
759	              ":\n    of the same kinds, with a return type that is a subtype of the other's under that correspondence.")
760	    }

763	    /* Drop the first element denoting the receiver type of the given type. */
764	    private def dropReceiver(param: Type) = param match {
765	      case STupleType(info, _::ty::Nil, None, Nil) => ty
766	      case STupleType(info, elements, varargs, keywords) =>
767	        STupleType(info, elements.takeRight(elements.size-1), varargs, keywords)
768	      case _ => NodeFactory.makeVoidType(NU.getSpan(param))

771	    def isDeclaredName(f: IdOrOpOrAnonymousName) = f match {
772	        case SId(_,_,str) => IdentifierUtil.validId(str)
773	        case SOp(_,_,str,_,_) => NU.validOp(str)
774	        case _ => false

778	        case SDeclaredMethod(_,_) => true
779	        case _ => false
780	    }
781	
782	    def isFunction(f: JavaFunctional) = f match {
783	        case SDeclaredFunction(_) => true
784	        case SFunctionalMethod(_,_) => true
785	        case SConstructor(_,_,_,_,_) => true
786	        case _ => false
787	    }
788	
789	    def isFunctionalMethod(f: JavaFunctional) = f match {
790	        case SFunctionalMethod(_,_) => true
791	        case _ => false
792	    }
793	
794	    def isDeclaredVariable(v: JavaVariable) = v match {

799	    private def mergeSpan(first: ArrowType, second: ArrowType): Span = mergeSpan(NU.getSpan(first), NU.getSpan(second))
800	
801	    private def mergeSpan(first: Span, second: Span): Span = new MultiSpan(first, second)
802	
803	    // whether a's declaration is written before b's: by file, then line, then column
804	    private def writtenBefore(a: ArrowType, b: ArrowType): Boolean = {
805	      val (x, y) = (NU.getSpan(a).getBegin(), NU.getSpan(b).getBegin())
806	      val (fx, fy) = (String.valueOf(x.getFileName()), String.valueOf(y.getFileName()))
807	      if (fx != fy) fx < fy
808	      else if (x.getLine() != y.getLine()) x.getLine() < y.getLine()
809	      else x.column() < y.column()
810	    }
811	
812	    /* Returns the type of the given list of parameters. */
813	    private def paramsToType(params: JavaList[Param], span: Span): Type =
814	      STypesUtil.paramsToType(toListFromImmutable(params), span) match {
815	        case Some(ty) => ty
816	        case _ =>
817	          val span = NU.spanAll(params)
818	          error(span,
819	                "Type checking couldn't infer the type of " + params)
820	          NodeFactory.makeVoidType(span)
821	      }
822	
823	    /* Returns the type of the given self type and a list of parameters. */
824	    private def paramsToType(self: Type, params: JavaList[Param], span: Span): Type = {
825	      val span = params.size match {
826	        case 0 => NU.getSpan(self)
827	        case _ => NU.spanAll(params)
828	      }
829	      val elems = toListFromImmutable(params).map(paramToType)
830	      if (elems.forall(_.isDefined))
831	        NodeFactory.makeTupleTypeOrType(span, toJavaList(List(self) ++ elems.map(_.get)))
832	      else {
833	        error(span,
834	              "Type checking couldn't infer the type of " + params)
835	        NodeFactory.makeVoidType(span)
836	      }
837	    }
838	
839	    private def error(loc: Span, msg: String) =
840	        errors = errors ::: List(TypeError.make(msg, loc))
841	
842	
843	    // The following is used by the ExportChecker.
844	
845	    def coverOverloading(set: Set[JavaFunction]) = {
846	      var result = Set[JavaFunction]()
847	      for (f <- set ; if !coveredBy(f, set)) {
848	        result = result + f
849	      }
850	      result = result.filter {
851	        case SDeclaredFunction(_) => true
852	        case _ => false
853	      }
854	      result.map { case SDeclaredFunction(fd) => fd }
855	    }
856	
857	    /*
858	     * Set may contain the object f; if so, ignore it.
859	     */
860	    private def coveredBy(f: JavaFunction, set: Set[JavaFunction]): Boolean = {
861	      var result = false
862	      for (g <- set ; if !result && f != g && coveredBy(f, g)) { result = true }
863	      result
864	    }
865	
866	    /* Whether the signature of f is covered by the signature of g */
867	    /* (If signatures are identical, then NOT covered; this is necessary for error reporting of duplicate definitions. */
868	    private def coveredBy(f: JavaFunction, g: JavaFunction): Boolean =
869	      globalOracle.lteq(f, g) && !globalOracle.lteq(g, f) && globalOracle.satisfiesReturnTypeRule(f, g)
870	
871	}

137	    // case (s,t) if (s==t) => pTrue() // moved up before cache for speed
138	    case (s: BottomType, _) => pTrue()
139	    case (s, t: AnyType) => pTrue()
140	    // Intersection types
141	    case (s, SIntersectionType(_,ts)) =>
142	      pAnd(ts.map(pSub(s, _)))  
143	    // An intersection bounds an inference variable from below as a whole
144	    case (s: IntersectionType, t: _InferenceVarType) => pLowerBound(t, s)
145	    case (SIntersectionType(_,ss), t) => {
146	//       val specialTerm =
147	//         if (ss.size > 0 && ss.exists(!_.isInstanceOf[ArrowType])) pTrue()
148	//         else pSub(NF.makeArrowType(NU.getSpan(x),
149	// 				   NF.makeIntersectionType(toJavaSet(ss.map(_.asInstanceOf[ArrowType].getDomain))),
150	// 				   NF.makeUnionType(toJavaSet(ss.map(_.asInstanceOf[ArrowType].getRange)))),
151	//                   t)
152	//       pOr(pOr(pOr(ss.map(pSub(_, t))), specialTerm),
153	//           pOr(Pairs.distinctPairsFrom(ss).map(tt => pExc(tt._1, tt._2)))) // The second constraint is the only time exclusion is called during subtype checking
154	      pOr(pOr(ss.map(pSub(_, t))),
155	          pOr(Pairs.distinctPairsFrom(ss).map(tt => pExc(tt._1, tt._2)))) // The second constraint is the only time exclusion is called during subtype checking
156	    }
157	    // Union types
158	    case (SUnionType(_,ss), t) =>
159	      pAnd(ss.map(pSub(_, t)))
160	    case (s: TraitType, t@SUnionType(_, ts)) =>
161	      val unionResult = pOr(ts.map(pSub(s, _)))
162	      comprisedTypes(s) match {
163	        case Some(cs) => pOr(unionResult, pAnd(cs.map(pSub(_, t)))) 
164	        case None => unionResult
165	      }
166	    // An inference variable below a union is bounded by the union as a whole: split,
167	    // a solution that holds only of the whole union, as a type variable bounded by
168	    // it, is lost, and the solver meets a disjunction it cannot unify.
169	    case (s: _InferenceVarType, t: UnionType) if !negate => pUpperBound(s, t)
170	    // A type variable is below a union where its bound is, as well as where it is
171	    // below one of the union's members.
172	    case (s@SVarType(_, id, _), t@SUnionType(_, ts)) if !negate =>
173	      val split = pOr(ts.map(pSub(s, _)))
174	      val hEntry = (negate, true, s, t)
175	      traits.readContext()
176	      if (history.contains(hEntry)) split
177	      else {
178	        val nHistory = history + hEntry
179	        val supers = pNorm(makeIntersectionType(toListFromImmutable(staticParam(id).getExtendsClause)))(nHistory)
180	        pOr(split, pSub(supers, t)(negate, nHistory))
181	      }
182	    case (s, SUnionType(_, ts)) =>
183	      pOr(ts.map(pSub(s, _)))
184	    // We must eliminate trait self types before making constraints  
185	    case (s: TraitSelfType, t) => pSub(removeSelf(s), t)
186	    case (s, STraitSelfType(_, named, _)) => pSub(s,named)
187	    // Inference variables
188	    case (s: _InferenceVarType, t: _InferenceVarType) =>
189	      pAnd(pUpperBound(s, t), pLowerBound(t,s))
190	    case (s: _InferenceVarType, t) => pUpperBound(s,t)
191	    case (s, t: _InferenceVarType) => pLowerBound(t,s)
192	    /* Type variables are special for several reasons
193	     *  1) Getting the bound out of a type variable is the only place where a type can increase in size during type checking.
194	     *     We use the history to ensure termination.
195	     *  2) They are the only place where you cannot negate using de Morgan's. There is a good explanation of why in the OOPSLA paper.
196	     */

198	        // || sid.asInstanceOf[Id].getText == tid.asInstanceOf[Id].getText
199	        ) => True
200	            
201	    case (s@SVarType(_, id, _), t) =>
202	      val hEntry = (negate, true, s, t)
203	      traits.readContext()
204	      if (history.contains(hEntry)) {
205	        False
206	      } else {
207	        val nHistory = history + hEntry
208	        val sParam = staticParam(id)
209	
210	        def stdResult () =  {
211	          if (negate) {        
212	//	               println("pSubInner 0: FALSE")
213			       pFalse()(!negate)
214			     } else {
215			       // Using pNorm causes the current history to be passed down
216			       val supers = pNorm(makeIntersectionType(toListFromImmutable(sParam.getExtendsClause)))(nHistory)
217	//	               println("pSubInner 1: supers = " + supers)
218			       pSub(supers, t)(negate, nHistory)
219	                     }
220	        }
221	        
222	        val result = 
223	          if (t.isInstanceOf[VarType]) {
224	        	  val v = t.asInstanceOf[VarType].getName()

226	              if (!lowerParam.getDominatesClause().isEmpty()) { 
227	                val lowers = pNorm(makeUnionType(toListFromImmutable(lowerParam.getDominatesClause)))(nHistory)
228	                pSub(s,lowers)
229	              } else {stdResult()}
230	        } else {stdResult()} 
231	        
232	        
233	//	ErrorMsgMaker.printHashCodes = true
234	//	println("...and the result of the recursive pSub is " + result)
235	//	ErrorMsgMaker.printHashCodes = false
236	        result
237	      }
238	    case (s, t@SVarType(_, id, _)) =>
239	      val hEntry = (negate, true, s, t)
240	      traits.readContext()
241	      if (history.contains(hEntry))
242	        False
243	      else {
244	        val nHistory = history + hEntry
245	        val sParam = staticParam(id)
246	        val result = if (negate) {
247			       // Using pNorm causes the current history to be passed down
248			       val supers = pNorm(makeIntersectionType(toListFromImmutable(sParam.getExtendsClause)))(nHistory)

250			       pSub(s, supers)(negate, nHistory)

252	//	               println("pSubInner 3: BOTTOM")

258	        result

262	    case (s: TraitType, t: TraitType) if (t==OBJECT) && !isLibraryIndex(s) => pTrue()
263	    
264	    case (STraitType(_,traitId_1,staticArgs_1,_),STraitType(_,traitId_2,staticArgs_2,_))

276	       else if (param.getVariance == -1)

282	     pAnd(formulas)
283	    
284	    //case (STraitType(_, n1, a1,_), STraitType(_, n2, a2, _)) if (typeCons(n1)==typeCons(n2)) =>
285	      // println("checking " + a1 + " vs " + a2)

287	    // A trait whose comprises clause lists a type at where-clause sizes, as
288	    // comprises { N[\n\] } where [\nat n\], is below t also when each listed

290	    // to its own size for that call.  A listed type extends the trait, so
291	    // the trait is opened once on each path.
292	    case (s: TraitType, t: TraitType) if opensSizes(s) =>
293	      val parentResult = withConditionalParents(s, pOr(parents(s).map(pSub(_, t))), pSub(_, t))
294	      val hEntry = (negate, true, s, t)
295	      traits.readContext()
296	      if (history.contains(hEntry)) parentResult

301	    case (s:TraitType , t: TraitType) =>

303	      val par = parents(s)
304	      // println(s + " has parents " + par)
305	      // A parent whose comprises clause lists types at a type where-clause variable
306	      // is not opened on the way up: s is one value, not every listed type.  A parent
307	      // that opens only sizes is opened as before.
308	      def throughParent(p: BaseType): CFormula = p match {
309	        case p: TraitType if opensTypes(p) && !(t.getName.getText == p.getName.getText) =>
310	          pOr(parents(p).map(pSub(_, t)))
311	        case p => pSub(p, t) }
312	      val parentResult = pOr(par.map(throughParent))
313	//       comprisedTypes(s) match {   // Gets a stack overflow error; maybe we don't need this in practice.  GLS 6/6/12

319	    // Arrow types
320	    case (SArrowType(_, d1, r1, e1, i1, _), SArrowType(_, d2, r2, e2, i2, _)) =>
321	      pAnd(pAnd(pSub(d2, d1), pSub(r1, r2)), pSub(e1, e2))
322	    // Tuple types
323	    // TODO: Handle keywords
324	    case (s@STupleType(_, e1, None, _), t@STupleType(_, e2, Some(mv2), _)) =>

326	    case (s@STupleType(_, e1, Some(v1), _), t@STupleType(_, e2, _, _)) =>
327	      pAnd(pSub(disjunctFromTuple(s, e1.size), disjunctFromTuple(t, e1.size)),

331	    // A tuple type whose element types are all subtypes of the library's Index is a subtype of Index.
332	    case (s@STupleType(_, e1, None, _), t: TraitType) if e1.nonEmpty && isLibraryIndex(t) =>

334	    case (s@STupleType(_, e1, _, _), t) =>
335	      pOr(e1.map(pEqv(_, BOTTOM)))
336	    case (s, t:TupleType) => 
337	      pSub(s, disjunctFromTuple(t,1))
338	    case _ => pFalse()
339	  }

420	  // dExc's answers in this analyzer, by the question with its inference variables renamed apart:
421	  // an answer is the same under every renaming of them, so a question asked again with fresh
422	  // variables, as each inference makes them, is computed once. An answer is kept only from an empty
423	  // cycle history, marked if its computation read the context, so that a hit on it is a read of the
424	  // context too, and shared through the trait table if it read none; a computation that opened a
425	  // size is not kept.
426	  private final val cacheExclusions = ProjectProperties.getBoolean("fortress.analyzer.exclusion.cache", true)
427	  private val exclusionMemo = new scala.collection.mutable.HashMap[(Type, Type), (Boolean, Boolean)]()
428	
429	  def dExc(x: Type, y: Type)(implicit history: Set[hType]): Boolean =
430	    if (!cacheExclusions || !history.isEmpty) isTrue(exc(x,y))
431	    else TypeAnalyzer.renamedApart(x, y) match {
432	      case None => isTrue(exc(x,y))
433	      case Some(question) => exclusionMemo.get(question) match {
434	        case Some((v, contextual)) => if (contextual) traits.readContext(); v
435	        case None => traits.sharedExclusion(question) match {
436	          case null =>
437	            val before = traits.contextReads
438	            val opened = openedSizeCount
439	            val result = isTrue(exc(x,y))
440	            if (openedSizeCount == opened) {
441	              val contextual = traits.contextReads != before
442	              exclusionMemo += (question -> (result, contextual))
443	              if (!contextual) traits.shareExclusion(question, result)
444	            }
445	            result
446	          case shared =>
447	            exclusionMemo += (question -> (shared.booleanValue, false))
448	            shared.booleanValue
449	        }
450	      }
451	    }

474	  protected def pExc(x: Type, y: Type)(implicit negate: Boolean, history: Set[hType]): CFormula = {
475	    if (x == y) pFalse()
476	    else if (cacheExcludes)
477	      traits.groundAnswer(false, x, y, negate) match {
478	        case null => pExcMemo.get((x, y, negate, history)) match {
479	          case Some(v) => traits.readContext(); v
480	          case _ =>
481	            val before = traits.contextReads
482	            val result = pExcInner(x,y)
483	            pExcMemo += ((x, y, negate, history) -> result)
484	            traits.ground(false, x, y, negate, before, result)
485	            result
486	        }
487	        case v => v
488	      }
489	    else pExcInner(x,y)
490	  }

492	  protected def pExcInner(x: Type, y: Type)(implicit negate: Boolean, history: Set[hType]): CFormula = (removeSelf(x), removeSelf(y)) match {
493	    case (s: BottomType, _) => pTrue()
494	    case (_, t: BottomType) => pTrue()
495	    case (s: AnyType, t) => pSub(t, BOTTOM)
496	    case (s, t: AnyType) => pSub(s, BOTTOM)
497	    case (s@SIntersectionType(_, elts), t) =>
498	      pOr(pSub(s, BOTTOM), pOr(elts.map(pExc(_, t))))
499	    case (s, t: IntersectionType) => exc(t, s)
500	    case (s@SUnionType(_, elts), t) =>
501	      pAnd(elts.map(pExc(_, t)))
502	    case (s, t: UnionType) => exc(t, s)
503	    case (i: _InferenceVarType, j: _InferenceVarType) if i==j => pFalse()
504	    case (i: _InferenceVarType, j: _InferenceVarType) => pAnd(pExclusion(i,j), pExclusion(j,i))
505	    case (i: _InferenceVarType, t) => pExclusion(i, t)
506	    case (s, j: _InferenceVarType) => pExc(j, s)
507	    case (s@SVarType(_, sid, _), t@SVarType(_, tid, _)) if (s==t || sid == tid) =>
508	      pOr(pSub(s, BOTTOM), pSub(t, BOTTOM))
509	    case (s@SVarType(_, id, _), t) =>
510	      val hEntry = (negate, false, s, t)
511	      traits.readContext()
512	      if (history.contains(hEntry))
513	        False
514	      else {
515	        val nHistory = history + hEntry
516	        val sParam = staticParam(id)
517	        val supers = pNorm(makeIntersectionType(toListFromImmutable(sParam.getExtendsClause)))
518	        if (negate) pFalse()(!negate) else pExc(supers, t)(negate, nHistory)
519	      }
520	    case (s, t:VarType) => exc(t, s)
521	    // TODO: Check what happens when stem s = stem t
522	    case (s: TraitType, t: TraitType) =>
523	      def checkEC(s: TraitType, t: TraitType): CFormula = {
524	        def cEC(s: TraitType, t: TraitType) = pOr(excludesClause(s).map(e => withClauseParams(e).pSub(t, e)))
525	        pOr(cEC(s, t), cEC(t, s))
526	      }
527	      def checkCC(s: TraitType, t: TraitType): CFormula = {
528	        def cCC(s: TraitType, t: TraitType): CFormula = {
529	          val scc = comprisesClause(s)
530	          pAnd(pFromBoolean(!scc.isEmpty), pAnd(scc.map(pExc(t,_))))
531	        }
532	        pOr(cCC(s, t), cCC(t, s))
533	      }
534	      def checkO(s: TraitType, t: TraitType): CFormula = {
535	        def cO(s: TraitType, t: TraitType): CFormula = typeCons(s.getName) match {
536	          case _:ObjectTraitIndex => pSub(s, t)(!negate, history)
537	          case _ => pFalse()
538	        }
539	        pOr(cO(s,t), cO(t,s))
540	      }
541	      def checkP(s: TraitType, t: TraitType): CFormula = {
542	        val sas = ancestors(s) ++ Set(s)
543	        val tas = ancestors(t) ++ Set(t)
544	        def cP(s: BaseType, t: BaseType): CFormula = (s, t) match {
545	          case (s@STraitType(_, n1, a1, _), t@STraitType(_, n2, a2, _)) if (n1 == n2) =>
546	            //Todo: Handle bool args
547	            pOr((a1, a2).zipped.map{
548	              case (STypeArg(_, _, t1), STypeArg(_, _, t2)) => pEqv(t1, t2)(!negate, history)

*
 *  Basically you can call the function reflect(n) and it will return
 *  an instance of NatParam.  But every instance of NatParam is an
 *  object N[\n\], so we can write a function which takes N[\n\] and
 *  pass it a NatParam; within that function n becomes a static nat
 *  parameter.
 *)
trait NatParam
  comprises { N[\n\] } where [\ nat n \]
  abstract getter toZZ() : ZZ32
end

value object N[\nat n\] extends { NatParam }
end

(* Actually convert a ZZ32 into a NatParam. *)
reflect(z:ZZ32):NatParam

content.content:
\section{Principles of Overloading}
\seclabel{principles-overloading}

Fortress allows multiple functional declarations of the same name to
be declared in a single scope.  However, recall from \chapref{names}
the following shadowing rules:
\begin{itemize}
\item
dotted method declarations shadow top-level function declarations with
the same name, and
\item
dotted method declarations provided by a trait or object declaration
or object expression
shadow functional method declarations with the same name that are
provided by a different trait or object declaration
or object expression.
\end{itemize}
Also, note that a trait or object declaration
or object expression must not have a
functional method declaration and a dotted method declaration with the
same name, either directly or by inheritance.
Therefore, top-level functions can overload
with other top-level functions and functional methods, dotted methods with
other dotted methods, and functional methods with other functional methods
and top-level functions.

Overloading functional declarations allows the benefits of polymorphic
declarations.  However, with these benefits comes the potential for
ambiguous calls at run time.  Fortress provides overloading rules for the
\emph{declarations} of functionals to eliminate the \emph{possibility}
of ambiguous calls at run time, whether or not these calls actually
appear in the program.

For each functional application expression, it should be a static error
if there does not exist a statically most applicable declaration for
that expression.
Furthermore, these rules are checked statically.
In fact, the overloading rules
in Fortress allow the compiler to identify the
statically most specific declaration for a particular call.  Therefore
an implementation strategy may be used in which the statically most
specific declaration is identified statically, and the runtime
dispatch mechanism need only consider dispatching among that
declaration plus declarations that are more specific than that
declaration (proof of this is given in \secref{proof-overloading-resolution}).
One case is an exception.
Where the static type of a call's argument stands between a trait with a
\KWD{comprises} clause and its listed types, several declarations applicable to
the static call may each have no other applicable declaration more specific
than them (\secref{more-specific-rule}).
Such a call is not a static error: it dispatches to a declaration no less
specific than each of them, and where they, and every declaration more specific
than them that the call may run, have no static parameters, its type is the
intersection of their return types (\secref{overloading-coercion-resolution}).
\revision{revival-meet}{The Working Draft of February 2011 knew no such call:
it read a \KWD{comprises} clause as saying which types are below a trait, where
\secref{trait-decls} now says which values belong to it, so that a trait with
static parameters may stand unlisted between a trait with a \KWD{comprises}
clause and its listed types.}

This chapter outlines several criteria for valid functional
overloading.  At any given program point, there is a set of overloaded
declarations that are in scope.  Fortress determines whether there is
a possibility for ambiguous calls from this set by comparing
declarations pairwise.  The following three sections each describes a
rule to accept a pair of overloaded functional declarations.  If a
pair of overloaded declarations satisfies any one of the three rules,
it is considered a valid overloading.

The overloading rules given in this chapter are disjoint.  That is, at
most one rule applies to each pair of overloaded declarations.  It is
possible for new rules to be added which allow additional
overloadings.

\label{adv-over-kwd}
Overloaded declarations may have different static parameters, or some of them
may have static parameters and others none (\secref{overloading-terms});
\secref{overloading-static-params} states how the rules of this chapter apply
to declarations with static parameters.  Valid overloadings for
declarations that contain keyword or
varargs parameters are determined
by analyzing the expansion of these declarations as described in
\secref{applicability-with-special-params}.  Therefore, keyword
parameters and varargs parameters are ignored in
the remainder of this chapter, and static parameters are ignored until
\secref{overloading-static-params}.
\revision{revival-overloading}{The Working Draft of February 2011 said here
that overloaded declarations must have static parameters that are identical up
to $\alpha$-equivalence, and ignored static parameters in the remainder of this
chapter.}

An operator method declaration whose name is one of the operator parameters
(described in \secref{opr-ident})
of its enclosing trait or object may be overloaded with other operator
declarations in the same component.  Therefore, such an operator method
declaration must satisfy the overloading rules
with every operator declaration in the same component.



In addition, a functional which takes a single parameter whose type is
a naked type parameter declared with the bound \TYP{Any} written, as
\EXP{T \KWD{extends} \TYP{Any}}, cannot be
overloaded.  This restriction prevents ambiguous overloadings such as
the following:
%makeSet[\T extends Any\](x: T): Set[\T\]
%makeSet[\T extends Any\](x: T, y: T): Set[\T\]

#!/bin/bash
# junit.sh <label> <dir-of-tests> <Name.test>... : the gather of climb batch N runs each .test through the
# harness in the main tree (fortress junit, the compiled test harness, as climb batch 6.5's gather ran its pair),
# in the order given, so that a link test runs before its XXX run test. Each named component's cache entries are
# removed before the list and after it. First line: the machine line (protocol.md, principle 2).
# ONE_JVM=1 (added 2026-09-29 for the repair on the merged tree, coordinator/climb-batch-workflow.md, "A repair
# of tests and records only"): the whole list in one fortress junit run, one JVM, as the gate's track runs them
# together; Shell junit hands the list to FileTests.suiteFromListOfFiles (Shell.java:1086), which puts its
# compile and link tests before its run tests (FileTests.java:997-1004), so a link test still runs first.
# The environment is env.sh's, set here without sourcing it, since env.sh also removes parser directories in
# /tmp. The tree is the one this script is in. FORTRESS_THREADS=4 is the pin of build.xml's fastTrack macro,
# which runs the gate's compiled tracks. The JVMs keep their temporary files, parser directories among them,
# in the tree's tmp/.
export JAVA_HOME=/usr/lib/jvm/java-25-openjdk-amd64
export PATH="$JAVA_HOME/bin:$PATH"
export FORTRESS_HOME="$(cd "$(dirname "$0")/../../../.." && pwd)"
unset JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS
export FORTRESS_THREADS=4
mkdir -p "$FORTRESS_HOME/tmp"
export JAVA_FLAGS="-Xmx4g -Xss64m -Djava.io.tmpdir=$FORTRESS_HOME/tmp"
FH=$FORTRESS_HOME; L=${1:?label}; D=$(cd "${2:?dir}" && pwd); shift 2
cd "$FH/ProjectFortress"
CP=$(../bin/fortress_classpath | tail -1)
echo "# junit.sh $L $(date -u +%FT%TZ); nproc $(nproc); $(grep -m1 'model name' /proc/cpuinfo | cut -d: -f2 | sed 's/^ //'); $(grep -m1 'cpu MHz' /proc/cpuinfo | cut -d: -f2 | sed 's/^ //') MHz; load at start $(cut -d' ' -f1-3 /proc/loadavg); $(java -version 2>&1 | head -1); FORTRESS_THREADS=$FORTRESS_THREADS; tree $(git -C $FH rev-parse --short HEAD)$(git -C $FH diff --quiet HEAD -- ProjectFortress Library || echo ' with the next rung applied, not yet committed'); tests from $D"
clean () { for t in "$@"; do n=$(sed -n 's/^tests=//p' "$D/$t" | head -1); [ -n "$n" ] && find ../default_repository/caches -name "*$n*" -exec rm -rf {} + 2>/dev/null; done; }
clean "$@"
if [ -n "${ONE_JVM:-}" ]; then
  files=(); for t in "$@"; do files+=("$D/$t"); done
  echo "########## [$L] fortress junit, one JVM: $*"
  java $JAVA_FLAGS -Dfile.encoding=UTF-8 -cp "$CP" com.sun.fortress.Shell junit "${files[@]}" 2>&1 | sed "s#$FH/##g" | grep -v '^\s*at ' | cut -c1-240
  echo "exit=${PIPESTATUS[0]}"
else
for t in "$@"; do
  echo "########## [$L] fortress junit $t"
  java $JAVA_FLAGS -Dfile.encoding=UTF-8 -cp "$CP" com.sun.fortress.Shell junit "$D/$t" 2>&1 | sed "s#$FH/##g" | grep -v '^\s*at ' | cut -c1-240
  echo "exit=${PIPESTATUS[0]}"
done
fi
clean "$@"
